content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper defines a "Black-box Knowledge Distillation" problem where "users only have access to the model predictions", instead of intermediate outputs. And proposed new distillation loss based on predictions only, which as reported outperforms the original "black-box" and even "white-box" method.
The contributions of this paper are:
1. Proposed prediction augmentation that map one prediction to multiple outputs by changing the temperature value in softmax.
2. Add batch/class-level alignment that minimize the MSE loss between correlation matrix of teacher output logits and student output logits among all predictions within a batch (batch-level)/all predictions of a class within a batch (class-level).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The approach is simple and very easy to implement.
2. The reported number looks significantly better than previous "black-box" method.

Weakness:
1. The "black-box" and "white-box" is just logits v.s features distillation. There is a distinguish in previous papers and it's not a definition of a new problem.
2. It does not look like a well-written paper, e.g. the title of algorithm 1 block is modified based on the DKD paper and it even still writes "Pseudo code of DKD in a PyTorch-like style". In Table 6, the reference to DKD is a question mark.
3. The augmentation looks too trivial and there should be more ablation study that prove it really works.
4. The result numbers reported in "white-box" model excluded DKD+ReviewKD with higher numbers, which is included in DKD paper.
5. The numbers are unreasonably high and I suggest to report the results averaged over multiple trials to make sure it's valid.

DKD:
Zhao, Borui, et al. "Decoupled Knowledge Distillation." CVPR'22

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper argues that knowledge distillation (KD) methods that require white-box access to the teacher’s intermediate features may not be applicable in practice due to commercial, privacy, or safety concerns. In these cases, black-box KD methods are required to train student models. However, existing black-box methods do not perform on par with white-box approaches, so stronger black-box methods are required.

To address this issue, the authors propose a novel black-box KD method, which expands on the original KD method (Hinton et al., 2015), by adding prediction augmentation, as well as batch-level and class-level alignment. In benchmarks, this method outperforms existing approaches both in student accuracy as well as training time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**

• The proposed black-box knowledge distillation method achieves state-of-the-art results on most benchmarks, while at the same time requiring much less time to train.

• The ablation studies show that all parts of the method contribute to the increased performance

• The paper is easy to follow, with clear figures and tables.

**Weaknesses:**

• The idea of distilling from a model that is only available via an API is not novel, similar problem settings are tackled in e.g. (Wang, 2021), which is not cited in the paper

• While the proposed method does not require access to intermediate features, it still needs access to the logits for all classes, which might not be available when the teacher is only accessible via an API. Thus, the target use-case for this method seems very narrow.

• The paper is missing an important black-box KD baseline, namely DKD (Zhao et al., 2022). When considering this baseline, the proposed method often performs only marginally better than existing black-box methods on CIFAR100 and ImageNet. For example, the proposed method achieves 72.19% Top-1 accuracy on CIFAR100 with ResNet56 as teacher and ResNet20 as student, and 71.62% accuracy on ImageNet with a ResNet34 teacher and a ResNet18 student. , and 73.01% accuracy with a ResNet50 teacher and a MobileNet-V2 student. Meanwhile, DKD achieves 71.97%(-0.22%) and 71.70%(+0.08%) accuracy in these settings. The claimed advantage in training time is also questionable when considering DKD. Furthermore, it seems that the authors are very much aware of DKD, given that they did include it in their comparison on MS-COCO. I would also suggest adding this work to the comparison.

**Reference**

Hinton, Geoffrey, Oriol Vinyals, and Jeff Dean. "Distilling the knowledge in a neural network." arXiv preprint arXiv:1503.02531 2.7 (2015).

Wang, Zi. "Zero-shot knowledge distillation from a decision-based black-box model." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.

Zhao, Borui, et al. "Decoupled Knowledge Distillation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Clarity and quality are good. Novelty seems to be marginal. Reproducibility seems not to be a problem.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is easy to follow, with clear figures and tables. The comparison results seem to be strong. However, there is an important reference method DKD missing, I suggest adding this method to the comparison and offering a comprehensive discussion regarding the improvements over DKD.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

Specifically, it proposes prediction augmentation and multi-level prediction alignment to enhance the performance of students. The logits of the student model will be enhanced by that of the teacher model in an instance, batch, and class level. Strength:
1. This work is well-written and easy to follow.
2. The performance of the proposed method seems good. 

Weaknesses：
1. Black-box KD is an important problem but my main concern is the definition of "black-box KD", for true black-box, only classification result is given, or top-5 results. Users cannot access the logits of teacher models, thus the proposed method is meaningless. So I think this work is not a strictly black-box KD.
2. Another concern is that the effect of the proposed method is only validated on ConvNet-based models but not compared with some new KD methods on Vision Transformer (ViT). So it would be better to prove the effects on both ConvNet and ViT.
3. This work is more like a technique report rather than a research paper, the technique is good but lacks enough novelty.

In Table 6, typo on the reference for DKD.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2425 by Reviewer 3CJf

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to perform the knowledge distillation using new practical tricks. It considers the distillation procedure done by making the student mimic the class probabilities of the teacher, and considers new ways to get more out of the teacher’s knowledge. The first idea is to perform augmentations in the logit space, where the student is asked to mimic not just the raw probabilities, but the student's scaled probabilities should match the scaled probabilities of the teacher as well. The second trick is to enforce the consistency between the teacher and student not just on the instance level, but also on batch and class level. The authors report that using these tricks can help the student perform better at image classification and object detection tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

- Overall, the combination of the three loss functions greatly help the student in terms of becoming better at the task at hand (e.g., Table 3/4). The individual components themselves are also shown to help the performance, showing the need for all three of them (Table 7).

- All the three components of the loss functions operate on the same feature level (class logits), i.e, they do not need to use features from different parts of the network to make things work.

- Even though the method is more complex than a typical distillation procedure in terms of the number of loss components, the overall training time is shown to be lower than some distillation methods. 

- If the priority is to get a more accurate student using the knowledge distillation, then the tricks introduced in this work will be useful to the community.


Weaknesses

- I do not understand the emphasis on the method being black box. Not because it is not accurate, but because it doesn’t seem to play that big of a role. The authors mention that for white-box distillation methods, one can use intermediate features. But it has been shown that the original distillation procedure, which is done on class logits, typically outperforms all other baselines. This was shown in CRD [1], which has been cited by the authors. The accurate tone of the paper should be about performing a more effective knowledge distillation.

- Even after the effectiveness of the proposed tricks, the paper pretty much reads like that; a collection of tricks which empirically improve the performance of the student. I would be fine with a simple fix to an existing distillation procedure which then improves the performance, as long as it was telling us something about the previous procedure; maybe there was an issue with the method which people had missed and this new way of doing the distillation fixes that.

- The batch-level alignment loss is a popular technique to distill knowledge. But the authors have not acknowledged that. In particular, in section 3.2.1, the authors should mention that the loss that they are explaining is already introduced in the Relational Knowledge Distillation [2], a paper that they have already cited in the related work section but not mentioned when Eq. 5 and 6 are being used.



References

[1] Contrastive Representation Distillation. Tian et al. ICLR 2020
[2] Relational Knowledge Distillation. Park et al. CVPR 2019.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The authors are clear in terms of what they wish to do; i.e, the components of the loss function are explained properly with appropriate mathematical notations. 

I do not think there is anything novel about the work, other than trying to extend the relational loss (borrowed from Relational knowledge distillation) for class-level alignment. 

The authors have given information which I believe will be sufficient to reproduce the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the tricks introduced in this work will definitely be helpful to the community from a practical perspective, especially prediction augmentation. That being said, I do not think this work offers anything concrete about the distillation process. For example, the effectiveness of prediction augmentation seems to imply that depending on what temperature value one uses, the information transferred to the student is different. Why is this the case? Does it simply help from a regularization point of view (smoother gradients)? Does it provide more information about the other classes? Because of these reasons, I do not feel our understanding of the distillation process improves. Hence, I recommend rejection.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
